## Libraries and data load

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(glmnet)
library(ranger)
library(tidyclust)
library(cluster)
library(readxl)
```

```{r}
final_raw <- read_csv("data/gapminder_final_F26.csv")
```

We study GDP per person (`gdp`) as the regression response and the four-category
world region (`world_4region`) as the classification response. We use the
remaining measurements as candidate predictors, apart from identifiers and
the exclusions explained below.

## Exploratory data analysis (EDA) part 1

### Checking for missing data

```{r}
countries <- final_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(population)) |>
  mutate(across(c(world_4region, landlocked, democracy, female_hos,
                  freedom_status, income_level, sexual_harassment), as.factor))
countries
```

The file has 273 geographic records, but 79 lack population and nearly all
other substantive measurements including territories and historical
entities. So we restrict the analysis to the 194 countries with population
data.

```{r}
missing_data <- final_raw |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Raw_missing") |>
  left_join(countries |>
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable",
                 values_to = "Country_missing"), by = "Variable") |>
  arrange(desc(Country_missing))
missing_data
```

Disregarding those 79 countries that have no records, energy use has 153 missing
values, and disaster deaths have 94. These are the clearest candidates for
removal before modeling.

### Units of variables

```{r}
variable_dictionary <- read_excel("data/Gapminder_Var_Dict_F26.xlsx") |>
  # Match variable names with the data we have
  mutate(Variable = recode(Variable, cell_phone = "cell_phones",
    corruption = "corruption_index", education = "education_index",
    electriciy_access = "electricity_access", sanitation_pct = "basic_sanitation"))
variable_dictionary
```

The table gives the supplied definitions and measurement years. GDP, CO2,
health spending, and alcohol are already per person; cell phones are per 100
people. Child mortality is per 1,000 live births, maternal mortality per 100,000
live births, and the murder, traffic, and suicide rates per 100,000 people.
Natural-disaster deaths are a total count, so we convert them to deaths per
100,000 residents.

```{r}
countries <- countries |>
  mutate(natural_disaster_rate = 100000 * natural_disaster_deaths / population)
```

### Logging variables

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 24
countries |>
  # Exclude categorical variables
  select(-c(geo, name, world_4region, landlocked, democracy, female_hos,
            freedom_status, income_level, sexual_harassment)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Original value", y = "Countries")
```

We use log10 transformations for those variables that have long upper tails.
This reduces the influence of very large values and gives more space to
differences among lower values.

```{r}
log_variables <- c("cell_phones", "child_mortality", "co2_per_capita", 
  "daily_income", "gdp", "health_spending_per_person", "maternal_mortality",
  "murder_rate", "natural_disaster_rate", "population", "poverty_rate",
  "traffic_deaths")
final_logged <- countries |>
  mutate(across(all_of(log_variables), log10))
```

```{r}
final_logged |>
  select(gdp, population, daily_income, co2_per_capita, child_mortality,
         health_spending_per_person, maternal_mortality, natural_disaster_rate) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "log10 value", y = "Countries")
```

## CV or testing/training for overfitting

```{r}
model_data <- final_logged |>
  select(-geo, -name, -energy_use_per_person, -natural_disaster_rate)
set.seed(2026)
final_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.8, strata = world_4region)
final_train <- training(final_split)
final_test <- testing(final_split)
tibble(Set = c("Training", "Testing"), Countries = c(nrow(final_train), nrow(final_test)))
```

We reserve about 20% of countries for testing and stratify by region to keep
all four regions represented. Country name, country code, and the two columns
above 40% missing are now excluded.
We plan to use 5 fold CV within training to choose tuning parameters.

## Variable selection comparison

## Clustering and PCA

### Which clustering method are you using? Which variable will you compare?

We use k-means and withhold world region until after choosing the number of
clusters.

### Missing values drop

```{r}
cluster_rows <- final_logged |>
  select(-geo, -energy_use_per_person,
         -natural_disaster_rate, -natural_disaster_deaths,
         -landlocked, -democracy, -female_hos,
         -freedom_status, -income_level, -sexual_harassment) |>
  drop_na()

cluster_data <- cluster_rows |>
  select(-name, -world_4region)

cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ ., data = cluster_data) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

The same two high-missingness variables - energy use and disaster deaths - are
excluded.

### Will you use categorical variables in your clusters?

We exclude all categorical variables, including region, from k-means and
PCA. Dummy coding is possible, but Euclidean distances would depend on how
many columns represent each category and on their frequencies. Using the
quantitative measurements keeps the distance definition simpler.

### Making clusters

```{r}
kmeans_spec <- k_means(num_clusters = tune()) |> set_engine("stats")
kmeans_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |>
  add_model(kmeans_spec)
cluster_grid <- tibble(num_clusters = 2:9)
full_data_resample <- rsample::apparent(cluster_data)
set.seed(2026)
kmeans_tuned <- tune_cluster(kmeans_workflow, resamples = full_data_resample,
  grid = cluster_grid, metrics = cluster_metric_set(sse_within_total))
cluster_quality <- collect_metrics(kmeans_tuned, summarize = FALSE)
cluster_quality
```

### Cluster quality

```{r}
best_k <- 3
set.seed(2026)
cluster_fit <- kmeans_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(tibble(num_clusters = best_k)) |>
  fit(data = cluster_data)
best_k
glance(cluster_fit)
tidy(cluster_fit)
```

### Check against hold out categorical variable

```{r}
cluster_results <- augment(cluster_fit, new_data = cluster_rows)
cluster_region <- cluster_results |> count(.pred_cluster, world_4region) |>
  group_by(.pred_cluster) |> mutate(Proportion = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup()
cluster_region
cluster_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = world_4region, fill = .pred_cluster)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "World region", y = "Proportion within region", fill = "Cluster")
tibble(Adjusted_Rand = mclust::adjustedRandIndex(cluster_results$.pred_cluster,
                                               cluster_results$world_4region))
```

Cluster 1 contains 46 African countries, 18 Asian countries, and four from
the Americas. Cluster 2 includes all 48 European countries but also 39
Asian, 31 American, and eight African countries. The adjusted Rand index
is 0.201, indicating limited agreement with the four geographic groups.
The grouping therefore captures a different structure from region labels.

### PCA

```{r}
pca_recipe <- cluster_recipe |>
  step_pca(all_predictors())
pca_prep <- prep(pca_recipe)
pca_scores <- bake(pca_prep, new_data = cluster_data)
pca_variance <- tidy(pca_prep, 2, type = "variance") |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance") |>
  mutate(Cumulative = cumsum(value))
```

PCA uses the same imputed and standardized quantitative matrix as k-means.

### Which components?

```{r}
pca_variance |> filter(terms == "percent variance")
pca_variance |> filter(terms == "cumulative percent variance")
pca_variance |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = component, y = value)) + geom_col() + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "PCA component", y = "Variation explained (%)")
```

PC1 explains 61.7% of standardized variation and PC2 another 7.6%,
giving about 69.3% together. Four components reach about 79.0%, while
five reach 82.5%.

### Loading/biplot

```{r}
pca_loadings <- tidy(pca_prep, 2)
pca_loadings |>
  mutate(component = fct_inorder(component)) |>
  filter(component == "PC1" | component == "PC2") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = terms, fill = terms)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) + facet_wrap(~ component) +
  labs(x = "Loading", y = NULL) + theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

These are the loading bars for the first two components. Variables with the same
sign on a component move together in thatm direction; opposite signs describe
opposing profiles.

PC1 contrasts higher HDI, GDP, daily income, and health spending on its
negative side with higher child mortality on its positive side. It
largely represents a development gradient. PC2 has positive loadings for
labor-force participation, alcohol, suicide, and the corruption index,
and a negative loading for electricity access.

### Compare to clusters

```{r}
pca_display <- pca_scores |>
  bind_cols(
    cluster_results |> select(.pred_cluster, world_4region)
  )
pca_display |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2,
             color = .pred_cluster, shape = world_4region)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Component 1", y = "Component 2", color = "Cluster")
```

Colors show the selected k-means clusters and shapes show the withheld
regions. Overlap of regions inside clusters would mean that similarity in
these quantitative profiles is not equivalent to geographic membership.
The cluster colors separate mainly along the development gradient on PC1,
while region shapes overlap.
